messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# James

James had been a bus driver for thirty-two years before the men came for him. He was sixty-one now, with a broad chest that had softened slightly with age, hands that knew the weight of a steering wheel through every season, and a reputation among his regular passengers for reliability—the kind of man who showed up, who kept his schedule, who could be counted on. That reputation had meant something to him. It had anchored him through a marriage that had weathered its own turbulence, through the small indignities of municipal employment, through the ordinary erosion of aging in a job that never quite paid what it should.

In 2003, during a humanitarian mission to Central America that he had volunteered for—a two-week stint helping to transport medical supplies to rural clinics—James had been taken from his hotel in a city whose name he had trouble holding in his mind now. The men who came for him had no clear demands. They were looking for American money, or leverage, or simply someone to hurt. What happened over the next four days existed in his memory as a series of fragments: the smell of the room, the specific angle of afternoon light through a high window, the texture of rope against his wrists, the sound of a voice—always that voice—asking questions in Spanish that he did not fully understand, and his own voice, hoarse and pleading, saying things he could not quite remember saying. The pain had been systematic and thorough. He had been waterboarded. He had been beaten. He had been left alone in the dark for hours. He had believed, at certain moments, that he would die there.

He had been released after four days when a local priest had intervened. He had returned to the United States. He had returned to his job. For the first few years, he had told himself it was over—a terrible interlude, something that had happened, something that he had survived. His wife, Maria, had wanted him to see someone, but James had resisted. He was not the kind of man who fell apart. He had gotten through it. He would get through this.

But the getting through had become harder. What James had come to believe, in the quiet hours when he could not sleep, was that he had failed in the most fundamental way. He had been helpless when he should have been strong. He had not fought hard enough, had not resisted with sufficient will, had not protected his own dignity or the dignity of the moment itself. The fact that he was one man against several, that resistance would have been futile, did not touch this conviction. He was certain now that weakness was not something that had happened to him in that room; it was something he was. This belief had seeped into how he understood everything that came after—every moment of fear, every startle response, every night when his body would not let him rest. His weakness explained it all. And because he was weak, because he had failed to be the man he should have been, he remained vulnerable in ways he could not quite articulate but felt with absolute certainty.

That vulnerability had become the texture of his nights. James found it harder to feel safe in darkness than in daylight, and the difference had widened over the years until night had become something he endured rather than experienced. He would lie awake beside Maria, listening for sounds—the creak of a door hinge, a car passing on the street, the neighbor's dog—and each sound would send a spike of adrenaline through his chest. Someone was entering the home. Someone was coming. His body knew this with the certainty of lived knowledge, and no amount of rational reassurance could quiet it. Maria had learned not to move suddenly in bed. She had learned to sleep on the far edge of the mattress, as if distance might help.

When memories surfaced—and they came without warning, triggered by a voice on the radio, the smell of a particular cleaning solution, the sensation of hands gripping his shoulders in a crowd—the terror returned intact, as vivid and overwhelming as if he were still in that room. But the memories themselves were incomplete, fractured. Some moments of the event remained crystalline: the exact pattern of shadows on the wall, the words of a prayer he had whispered, the weight of his own thirst. Other stretches had simply vanished, leaving gaps that his mind could not or would not cross. This fragmentation haunted him. The missing pieces felt like evidence of how badly he had broken, how thoroughly the experience had shattered something essential. And each time he tried to remember, each time a fragment surfaced and brought the terror with it, it reinforced his conviction that he had been fundamentally weak—that a stronger man would have endured differently, would have remembered more clearly, would not be sitting here at sixty-one, unable to sleep in his own bed, listening to the house settle around him as if it were a threat.

The cycle had tightened over the years. His conviction that he was weak, that he had failed, that he could not have done anything differently and yet should have—this belief made every sensation of threat feel more real, more confirming. And every night of vigilance, every startle response, every moment when his body reacted before his mind could catch up, seemed to prove the belief true. He was broken. He was still in danger. The danger was inside him now, and he could not escape it because it was him.

Six months ago, Maria had finally insisted. She had found him one morning on the kitchen floor, having gotten up at three in the morning and simply stayed there, unable to return to bed, unable to move. She had called their primary care physician. The physician had referred him to a trauma specialist. James had resisted for weeks, but Maria had been firm in a way she had not been about many things in their marriage, and James, despite everything, did not want to lose her. He had made an appointment. He had sat in a waiting room full of magazines he did not read, waiting to be called in, wondering if talking about what had happened would make it worse, wondering if a therapist would see what he saw—a weak man who had failed when it mattered most, who deserved the nights he endured, who would never forgive himself for the person he had become.
